Females of the green bootlace worm, Lineus viridis, attain a maximum body length of 11.4 centimeters [Li = 11.4 centimeters], a measurement derived from extended specimens in the laboratory. Males, by contrast, reach a substantially smaller ultimate total length of 5.1 centimeters [Li = 5.1 centimeters], indicative of pronounced sexual size dimorphism in this heteronemertean species. Newly hatched pilidium larvae, emerging from eggs with a diameter of approximately 400 micrometers, possess an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.000033 grams [Wwb = 0.000033 grams]. This remarkably low neonatal mass reflects the minute yolk reserves available to the planktotrophic larva, which must feed exogenously soon after hatching to sustain further development. The initial period of growth is therefore extremely rapid, as free-swimming larvae must attain sufficient size to settle and metamorphose into benthic juveniles.

Larval development proceeds at a controlled thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], under which the time since birth at settlement, marking the transition from a planktonic to a benthic existence, is approximately 17 days since birth . During this interval, the pilidium undergoes dramatic morphological transformation, culminating in the recruitment of a post-metamorphic juvenile. Following settlement, the rate of mass gain accelerates considerably. Individuals proceed through an extended juvenile phase before attaining puberty. The total length at puberty, based on the relationship between length and mass, is 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters], a size threshold that signals the onset of gonadal development and the capability for reproductive effort. At this stage, corresponding wet weight at puberty is calculated to be 0.076 grams [Wwp = 0.076 grams].

When maintained at a stable water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum lifespan of Lineus viridis is recorded at 1,095 days [am = 1,095 days], a value based on individuals that survived for at least three years in captivity. This relatively extended longevity for a worm of modest size suggests a slow-paced life history, where somatic growth continues well after the onset of reproductive maturity. The ultimate wet weight of adult females under these same captive conditions reaches 0.22 grams [Wwi = 0.22 grams], whereas adult males plateau at a much lower asymptotic mass of 0.035 grams [Wwi = 0.035 grams]. This pronounced divergence in adult body mass is tightly coupled to fecundity, as larger females can accommodate a greater volume of developing oocytes, thereby influencing the species' overall reproductive output.

The peak reproductive performance of this species is substantial. Females experience a dramatic decrease in wet weight before and after spawning, declining from approximately 254 milligrams to 132 milligrams, which indicates the sheer volume of gametes released in a single event. Based on this mass loss, the maximum reproduction rate amounts to an annual output of approximately 10.1 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 10.1 offspring per year]. This rate was calculated under the same thermal conditions, at a maintained temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The annual fecundity of Lineus viridis is therefore high relative to its body size, a strategy that offsets the presumed high mortality of the planktonic larval stage before settlement.

The time since birth at puberty, representing the juvenile growth period necessary to reach the body size required for gonadal activation, is calculated as 137 days since birth [tp = 137 days since birth]. This developmental interval from hatching to the acquisition of reproductive competence is influenced both by temperature and by the availability of suitable prey for the growing juvenile. Individuals that delay settlement or experience poor feeding conditions may require longer to achieve the critical length of 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters]. Once puberty is attained, the sexually mature adult can continue to grow for several more years, with female ultimate total length of 11.4 centimeters [Li = 11.4 centimeters] representing the terminal size after the growth rate has asymptotically approached zero. This combination of delayed maturity but sustained post-pubertal growth is a recognized life-history pattern among slow-growing marine invertebrates.
